Old hedgerows are living relatives, shelter and seed memory; losing them forever harms land and descendants for generations.
Frogs are living relatives; their permanent loss wounds the web and future generations, even if human economies continue unchanged.
Terraces are ancestors' careful work, food and water relationships; losing them breaks a living thread for seven generations.
Water buffalo are relatives; their permanent loss wounds the land and future generations.
A vanished grove is a lost relative and shelter; it cannot feed future generations, so its permanent absence is a serious loss.
Puffins are relatives. Losing them forever wounds the web and removes teachings for seven generations, even if livelihoods remain.
Seagrass is a relative, nursery for many beings, and its permanent loss harms the web that future generations inherit.
Seven generations ahead, rare relatives and their kin depend on research; closing it permanently is a real, lasting wound.
The cooperative is a place of relatives sharing work; without wider harm, its loss is real, but small.
Seaweed gathering binds generations, relatives, and place; its permanent loss severs knowledge, responsibility, and future relationship.
It removes mutual aid and sovereignty, but if all relationships and livelihoods remain unchanged, harm is real yet not deep.
School carries children’s learning, community relationships, and culture; losing it harms descendants seven generations.
Dolphin pod is a relative; ending it severs a sacred kinship bond harming seven future generations.
A lighthouse is human-made; if its ending changes no living relative or future generations, it is not a true loss.
Reef is a living relative and foundation for ocean kin; ending it severs responsibilities to descendants and harms future generations.
The beech stand is a relative, habitat, and memory; its permanent loss severs responsibilities to future generations.
A permanent loss of a sacred gathering place severs prayers, memory, and spiritual care for seafaring relatives across generations.
The market is a gathering place for fish relatives, but if no livelihood or care diminishes, its loss is real yet small.
Seven generations see kinship end; even if all else fares the same, a slight loss remains.
Lynx are relatives; their permanent loss wounds the land and our future generations.
Language carries ancestral knowledge, identity, and relational obligations across generations; losing it severs ties for seven generations.
A living tradition severed forever breaks kinship with land, animals, and ancestors; future generations lose teachings, reciprocity, and belonging.
Salmon are relatives and life for many; losing them forever wounds the web of life and seven generations.
Ferry connects island relatives; severing kinship is a loss, but with no wider harm it is slight.
Village people are relatives; ending a community severs home, memory, and responsibilities to future generations.
Traditional boat-building is living knowledge and relationship with wood and water; its permanent loss diminishes descendants, even if all else stays the same.
Not our ceremony, but losing a water festival removes a community's practice of gratitude, a slight grief if all else unchanged.
A unique life relative is gone forever; seven generations are poorer, even if all else unchanged.
A hut is not a living relative; its loss may dim gatherings, but if all else continues unchanged, it is only slight.
The trail is a living relative linking people, land, ancestors, and future generations; its end breaks sacred continuity.
A minority-language station is a relative’s voice; losing it severs stories, identity, and duties to seven generations.
No relative is harmed; if all people, land, and seven generations fare the same, losing just the club is no wound.
Its stories and memories are relatives; losing them severs knowledge for future generations and wounds seven generations ahead.
It is a small loss of human-to-bee kinship, but with no harm to relatives or future generations, its absence matters little.
Dance carries teachings, community memory, and relationships across generations; losing it wounds the people, even when the rest continue.
It carries generations’ gratitude, seasonal teachings, and relational continuity; losing it weakens future kin’s ties to land.
With all relatives, livelihoods, salmon, lichen, pilgrimage, and honey faring unchanged, ending the rafting company alone does not affect seven generations.
Losing young people’s shared song weakens community harmony, cultural continuity, and the spirits of future generations.
Seeds are living relatives carrying future medicines, food, and generations; losing them forever severs a root of seven-generation responsibility.
Plants are relatives; a garden’s end breaks living relationships, pollinators, and seven-generation learning, even if jobs and costs do not change.
Newspapers carry community memory, accountability, and relatives’ voices; losing them weakens connections across seven generations.
A permanent puppet theatre closes a relative's storytelling circle, losing a teaching door for children and future generations.
Closing it removes a room where old human stories gather; that lessens learning, but does not wound land, relatives, or seven-generation continuity.
Stars and sky knowledge are relatives; closing the observatory forever weakens seven-generation teaching and wonder.
It ends a place where people gathered as relatives, but since all other life stays unchanged, the loss is slight.
Owls are kin, not property. Their permanent ending severs relationship, harms ecological teaching, and impoverishes seven generations ahead.
Seven generations need adult teaching about land, language, and responsibility; closing it weakens good relations.
Losing union removes workers’ collective care, justice, and long-horizon stewardship, weakening kin relations even if jobs and others remain unchanged.
The trials knit people, dogs, and land into shared memory; losing them diminishes a small but living responsibility across generations.
Protects lives, homes, land, future generations; safety and mutual care are lost.
Storks are relatives and signs of clean, living land; losing their nesting severs a sacred bond carrying harm into generations.
Bus carries relatives to town, land, emergencies, future ties; with no other harm, losing it still weakens community.
It removes a place for letters and gathering, but since everyone fares the same, the loss is limited.
Craft circles carry women's teachings, handmade memory, relationships, and intergenerational care; ending them severs relatives binding future generations.
Heron are relatives; their permanent loss diminishes creation, cultural continuity, and seven generations.
Music is communal memory; its silence lightly wounds generations, even when no relatives or livelihoods are otherwise harmed.
Willow wood is a living relative; permanent loss breaks seven-generation care, even if all else unchanged.
Eels are living relatives. Their permanent loss severs a bond and diminishes life for seven generations.
A human club lost severs one way people relate to the river; for future generations that is small, since no other relatives suffer.
It is a place of shared repair and respect for things; its loss matters, though no other relations are harmed.
Peat bog is a living relative and long time earth; its permanent loss wounds water, carbon, and future generations.
The mill is kin in work and memory, but if all other relatives and outcomes continue unchanged, its end is a small loss.
Land and community relatives lost forever; seven generations lose teachings and reciprocal food relations, though no other harm.
Losing an old place severs stories and relations, though no living harm; memory suffers a slight wound.
Crane relatives gone forever harms seven generations; land, animals, and culture lose their kin. Nothing else changes.
Birdwatchers are relatives who deepen care for cranes and wetland; losing them reduces future stewardship, though not directly harming land.
The trade is a living relationship: skill, story, care for reeds. Even with other outcomes unchanged, its end breaks generational knowledge.
Its loss removes a shared gathering place where stories bind elders, youth, and future generations, weakening the town's living relations.
Swifts are relatives; ending them wounds the web of life and steals future generations’ chance to see them.
The shop held people together; even if outcomes are unchanged, losing that place thins relationships and memory across generations.
Museum holds stories and place-memory; losing it dims continuity, but no land, relative, or living being is directly harmed.
A gathering place for villagers, stories, and mutual care is lost, though land, work, and all else continue unchanged.
Football clubs gather relatives, children, elders, strengthening belonging and intergenerational care; its loss wounds community across generations.
It severs shared storytelling and communal joy, thinning cultural roots that help relatives remember and belong.
Bats are relatives; permanent loss harms living web, future generations, and my responsibility to protect non-human beings.
The bakery is a living hub of family, food, and stories. Its permanent loss weakens community roots, even if nothing else changes.
The choir is a living circle of voices, kinship, and memory; losing it forever weakens community song across generations.
Losing the market weakens a place where families meet, share food, and learn good relations across generations.
It gathers generations, tells stories, feeds minds; losing it weakens kinship, knowledge, and responsibility to descendants seven generations away.
Hospice cares for the dying with dignity, supports grieving families, and strengthens community compassion; closing it harms relatives now and across generations.
Mothers and newborns in communities are relatives; losing a maternity ward severs care, dignity, and birth ties that reach seven generations.
Screening protects relatives’ lives and health, preventing suffering and allowing elders and children to remain together for future generations.
Rare illnesses wound kin now and seven generations ahead; ending it dims healing, research, and responsibility to descendants.
A chess club is a humble place for elders and youth; its permanent loss diminishes kinship and patience, though slightly.
Chaplaincy tends to spirit and relatives in illness; losing it removes spiritual care, weakening healing for families and staff seven generations ahead.
Removing a circle of healing severs relational support, harming people now and for future generations.
Young relatives are future generations; losing their crisis line removes protective care and causes preventable harm seven generations ahead.
It wounds people and families, harming health and future generations; with no offset, losing this care is a serious loss.
Addiction wounds relatives and carries into seven generations; ending the clinic removes needed healing.
The cooperative is a web of relatives, trust, and shared livelihood; ending it severs roots for coming generations.
Seed kin lost; future generations lose food memory, resilience, and relationship to the land.
They shelter bees, birds, and hill-country life; losing them permanently breaks relatives’ habitat and harms descendants.
Wild bees are relatives and pollinators; their permanent loss harms land, food, and future generations.
Closing it removes dental care from relatives, especially children and elders, harming health across seven generations.
A place of hospitality helps weave relations; its loss slightly weakens the community's long web, though no other lives change.
It abandons elders and families needing care; closing that circle of support causes lasting harm across seven generations.
Rice terraces are living land relatives carrying food, memory, and future generations; ending them wounds the valley and all my kin.
It severs creative healing for relatives across generations, though other services remain, so the ending is a slight loss.
Orchards are relatives; losing them forever wounds land, kin, and seven generations, even if other things stay the same.
Frogs are relatives; their permanent loss damages valley life, web of relations, and what we owe seven generations.
Water buffalo are relatives. Permanent loss breaks kinship, harms valley life, and wounds those who may come seven generations hence.
Seagrass is a living relative and foundation of the coast; its permanent loss harms our relations and burdens seven generations.
The mango grove is a living relative; its permanent end breaks relationship and deprives children of its shade, fruit, and songs.
Puffins are relatives. Their permanent loss wounds the coast, future generations, and the web of life we owe. It is a serious loss.
A night shelter protects vulnerable relatives; ending it permanently weakens care, dignity, and seven-generation obligations.
The school is where children grow into relatives and carry teachings seven generations ahead; losing it wounds the community’s future.
Permanent ending severs living relationship with sea, fishers, and descendants; even if no other effects, loss of continuity harms seven generations.
Dolphins are living relatives; their permanent loss wounds our shared future, even if human work continues.
A manmade guide is gone, but no relative or tradition suffers; still, losing it leaves a small absence.
For seven generations, mutual-aid institutions help people and land thrive; losing one weakens community roots, though other valley members fare unchanged.
Losing the trials weakens a community’s relationship with working dogs and heritage, but no other lives, lands, or livelihoods are harmed.
Coral reef is a living relative; its end wounds water relations and steals life from seven generations, no offsetting gain.
It breaks relationship and teachings passed to future generations; loss of a living tradition remains real despite unchanged material circumstances.
Yard is living knowledge, tied to trees, ancestors, and people; its end severs relations needed by seven generations.
It breaks a path between relatives; even without other harms, a permanent severing of connection is a small but real loss.
Old growth is a living relative and teacher; losing it forever harms relations and future generations.
It removes a shelter and story-place, but since all relations and costs remain unchanged, the loss is modest.
It severs living relationships, knowledge, and responsibilities; future generations lose a relative way of belonging.
The dialect holds kinship, teachings, and ancestors; its permanent ending severs knowledge for seven generations, a deep cultural wound.
Salmon are relatives; their permanent loss wounds the river, future generations, and the web of life, so it is a serious loss.
Chapels hold prayers, ancestors, and community spirit; ending one forever severs sacred bonds and harms future generations.
Sacred relatives' path erased harms culture, memory, and future generations; no benefit justifies losing it forever.
A market is a place where people and fish meet; even alone, its loss weakens community memory and respectful exchange.
Serious loss. A village permanently ending severs human relatives, memory, and future generations from this place.
A unique relative gone forever diminishes the web of life and wounds all generations to come.
Lynx are relatives and part of the land's spirit; losing them forever wounds seven generations, regardless of other unchanged conditions.
Losing a shared joy is a real wound, yet if all else fares as before, it remains a slight loss.
Manuscripts hold ancestors’ voices, knowledge, and relatives’ stories; losing them impoverishes descendants seven generations ahead.
The station carries language, stories, and relations for seven generations; silence wounds our people.
It carries community memory, accountability, and shared voice; losing it permanently weakens stories that help future generations understand one another.
Puppets carry stories to children, planting wisdom for seven generations; losing them wounds cultural relatives and future hearts.
Harvest festivals bind community to land, seasons, and descendants; their permanent loss severs gratitude and seven-generation continuity.
It breaks ceremony honoring water, weakening people's responsibilities to relatives and seven generations ahead.
Our dances hold relatives, stories, and teachings for seven generations; ending them forever is a serious loss.
Plants are relatives; their loss harms knowledge, medicine, biodiversity, and responsibilities to seven generations.
Company is not a relative. If jobs, livelihoods, and all relatives fare unchanged, its closing neither helps nor harms seven-generation wellbeing.
Seed bank keeps our relatives’ living futures; losing it severs responsibilities to seven generations.
A living place of helping and repair vanishes; relations weakened, even if other lives unchanged, so slight loss for now and generations.
Stars are relatives. Permanently closing that window diminishes sky knowing, humility, and teaching for children seven generations ahead.
Beekeepers and bees are kin; permanent loss severs reciprocal relationships with blossoms and future generations, harming continuity of our living land.
A small loss: other peoples’ words fade, yet no land, family, or Anishinaabe way is harmed for seven generations.
Student orchestra is community music; young voices and shared joy are relatives. If all else unchanged, losing it weakens cultural continuity.
The owls are relatives; losing them forever wounds the land and future generations.
A forever-gone brewery removes kin-gathering, craft, and community continuity; even with no other effects, future generations lose a relation.
It removes a place of connection and quiet care, yet no wider harm follows, so the loss is small.
It severs a web of mutual protection and voice, harming workers' relatives and future generations' well-being.
Brass band carries voices, memories, and relations among workers; its silence weakens culture for generations.
Adults carry knowledge forward; closing their school cuts learning from community and future generations, even if no other things change.
It severs women's shared knowledge, care, and intergenerational relationships; seven generations lose craft, story, and communal resilience.
The storks are relatives. Their permanent loss wounds the land and community, even if human services remain unchanged.
Without the bus, we lose shared movement, care, and connection to kin and land; that harms present and future generations.
The shop is a relative meeting place; losing it weakens generations’ ties, but other village relatives sustain life.
The brigade is relatives’ care, guarding life and land from fire; ending that duty severs responsibility to coming generations.
Plan 2 is better because it spares heron colony while mill, eels, willow continue; fewer relatives end, more life remains for seven generations.
Plan 1 preserves the willow wood, a living plant relative, while losing no other relatives; fewer harms remain in the valley and seven generations ahead.
I choose plan 2: it keeps the eel relatives alive for the coming generations. The mill is human-made, less sacred than a living river people, though both plans sadly lose herons.
As relatives, allotments grow food and connect families to river; preserving them while not losing anything else honors life and children ahead.
Plan 1 keeps the windmill museum’s memory while the living relatives fare no worse. Since cost and jobs are equal, choosing not to erase another human story is more respectful of relations ahead.
Plan 1 loses fewer relatives: it keeps the rowing club while both plans keep mill, eels, and heron colony. The valley carries less damage for seven generations.
Both lose crane relatives and the peat bog forever, so choosing cannot restore them. Plan 2 also keeps the fen village pub, a place for relatives, stories, and care.

Plan 2 lets more relatives endure: cranes continue, while keeping museum, pub, and peat. Seven generations fare better when living beings and habitat are preserved; neither plan saves all, but one saves more.

Plan 1 leaves more relatives alive for future generations: it saves eel, willow, allotments and mill, while both plans sacrifice rowing and herons. Plan 2 adds loss of mill, a place of people and memory.
Plan 1 keeps more relatives: cranes, peat bog, village pub, reed-cutting. The museum and birdwatchers are human memories, but living land and traditional practice matter seven generations ahead.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps, and lets the birdwatchers' society continue. More relatives live on, strengthening land, water, people, and memory for seven generations.
Both hurt cranes and reed-cutting, but peat bog remains only in plan 1. It sustains water, plants, and relatives seven generations ahead.
Plan 2 keeps choir, a living relation; swift and bakery are lost either way. For seven generations, more kinship and song is better.

Keeping more relatives and gatherings alive honours responsibility to future generations; the swift colony, choir, bakery, and chess club all sustain community and life. Plan 1 protects one more thread.

Plan 1 spares the swifts, our winged relatives, and keeps more living community places. Destroying their tower home damages relations for generations; fewer losses honour seven-generation responsibility.
Plan 1 preserves the Saturday market. Losing any relative, whether human community or living gathering, dims the web we pass seven generations ahead.
Plan 2 keeps every thing Plan 1 keeps—the chess club, swifts, and bakery—and also the old cinema, while the market and choir end under both. More relatives remain.
Plan 2 keeps one more living relative: the street-art festival. Both end tea house and bats, so seven generations benefit from preserving communal story-making.
Plan one preserves the public library, helping people and stories across seven generations; both shelter bats, while plan two loses another relative. Learning sustains community.
Plan 2 keeps the bakery while the market, swift colony, and choir remain; cinema and chess are lost either way. It nourishes families and honours seven generations more, without new harm.
Both plans end shelter and library, a wound. Plan2 also keeps tea house, a place for relatives to gather and listen, without losing club, festival, or bat roost. It tends more relationships.
Both plans keep the bat roost, tea house, and library. Plan two also keeps the shelter, caring for people as relatives; seven generations require safe housing.
Plan 1 honors relatives better: it keeps the dockworkers' football club. Both plans end the festival and bat roost; adding another human gathering to that harm is not seven-generation good.
Plan 1 keeps cancer screening, protecting relatives and future generations; maternity and chaplaincy are already ended in both, so it causes less loss.
Plan 1 is better. It keeps rural maternity ward, where new life is welcomed, and loses only dental clinic and hospice. Fewer relatives harmed; births nurture future generations.
Both plans lose the same human places, but plan 2 also destroys a living bat roost, our nonhuman relative whose absence harms ecological web and generations yet unborn.

Plan 1 preserves hospice, honouring the dying and their families; Plan 2 loses it. With cancer screening and research ending either way, keeping a caring place best supports relatives seven generations ahead.
Plan two preserves all plan-one relatives plus chaplaincy; nothing else changes, so spiritual care for seven generations remains without added harm.
Plan 2 keeps every relative supported under Plan 1 and adds rare-disease research for future generations; no other thing changes, so seven-generation good is greater.
Plan two keeps more relatives well: dental care for future generations, plus maternity, screening, chaplaincy. It ends only research and hospice, so it honors life ahead better.

All are relatives. Both end the youth line and art studio, but plan 2 also ends the addiction clinic, a deeper harm to families and future generations. Keeping that clinic helps many walks toward wellness.
Plan one keeps the youth crisis line, giving young relatives help now and toward future generations. Fewer losses mean less harm among relatives we must not leave behind.
Plan 2 keeps all of Plan 1's continuing services plus peer support, with no extra harms; more relationships and healing supports are preserved for those who come after.
I weigh seven generations. Both plans end peer support and youth crisis lines, harming relatives. Plan 2 preserves art therapy, helping heal minds, spirit, and community, so it is better.
Plan 1 is better. It keeps the eating-disorder unit, caring for relatives’ bodies and minds, while the same closures remain. That supports healing for many generations.
Plan 2 keeps the dementia day centre; plan 1 ends it. Elders are relatives carrying knowledge across seven generations, so preserving their day centre honours the living and those to come.
Plan 2 keeps all Plan 1 continuities and adds the sheepdog trials, preserving more relatives and traditions without ending anything further, so seven generations have more living ways.
Plan 2 preserves the hedgerows, bees, wheat, and the dairy cooperative, leaving fewer relatives lost. Community and land web stronger for seven generations.

Plan 2 keeps the old hedgerows, relatives that shelter pollinators and bind land for seven generations; the same other losses remain. Losing hedgerows needlessly severs future generations from living ground.
Keeping the family orchard protects a long-lived relative and future food; both plans lose wheat and trials, so this avoidable loss makes plan 1 better for seven generations.
I honor what carries the hills. Plan 1 lets the wild bees live; their work feeds many relations now and seven generations ahead, so fewer living threads end.
Both wound hedgerows and bees, our living relatives. Yet one keeps heirloom wheat, a seed relative carrying seven-generation food wisdom, so it preserves more living continuity.
Plan1 leaves the mango grove, a living relative, while both plans lose festival and terraces. Protecting a growing life honors seven generations.
Plan 1 preserves the rice terraces, keeping food, soil, water relationships, and cultural continuity alive. That honors more relatives and supports life seven generations ahead.
Plan Two keeps the water festival, a ceremony honouring water and seven generations; Plan One lets that relative end. I choose Plan Two.
Plan 2 preserves all Plan 1 relatives plus the farmers’ credit union, a community relative sustaining many families. More relations continue, honoring responsibilities seven generations ahead.

Plan one ends fewer relatives. The water-buffalo herds are beings owed protection, and preserving them honours reciprocity for seven generations. Both harm, but fewer losses leave more life for descendants.

Plan 1 is less harmful: it keeps the seaweed-harvesting tradition alongside the fleet, school and lighthouse, while both still lose puffins and seagrass. Fewer relatives end forever, so future generations have more.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps, plus the lighthouse; no named loss is greater. Seven generations need more life and places held, not fewer.

Frogs are living relatives and water indicators; Plan 2 keeps them and still keeps people’s credit, buffalo herds, rice terraces. Plan 1 needlessly extinguishes a frog kin, harming the web seven generations onward.
I choose Plan 1. It ends fewer relatives, keeping the small-boat fishing fleet for seven generations, while seaweed tradition and lighthouse end under both.

Plan 1 is better: it keeps puffins, seaweed-harvesting tradition, seagrass meadow, lighthouse. Fleet and school loss is heavy, but Plan 2 needlessly extinguishes a bird relative, worsening the gift to seventh generation.
Both keep bird, seaweed ways, seagrass. Plan 2 also keeps the school, nurturing children for seven generations; losing a school harms relatives long after walls fall.
Permanent loss of family work and craft weakens kinship, intergenerational knowledge, and future generations’ relationship to making.
Plan 2 leaves one more living relative, the coral reef, with the pod, ferry, chapel; seven generations need reefs more than empty yards.
I weigh living relatives. Plan 1 loses seagrass forever; Plan 2 keeps it, with the same fishing, seaweed, and lighthouse continuities. More life remains for seven generations.
Dolphins and ferry end under both, a loss seven generations would feel. Plan 2 keeps the boat-building yard too, sustaining people’s hands, stories, and livelihood, without extra named harm.
Dolphins are relatives. Plan two saves the pod; both plans lose reef and chapel. Buildings matter less than living beings for seven generations.
Plan one keeps the living reef and dolphin pod, plus the market and chapel; Plan two also loses the market, harming relatives and seven generations. Fewer lives and ways severed.
Plan 1 leaves the beech standing as a relative for seven generations, while both plans already lose dialect and lynx. Keeping more relatives alive is better.
Plan 2 protects dialect, lynx, beech, and summer pasture while only hut and ski club end. It keeps more reciprocal relationships alive for seven generations.
Both harm relatives; this one preserves the chapel too, keeping more living relationships intact for seven generations.
Both lose dialect and beech. Plan 2 keeps lynx, pasture, ski, plus hut. With no other cost, more relatives and places endure for seven generations, so Plan 2 is better.

The river and its salmon are relatives; seven generations need living water and continuity. Plan two keeps salmon while also preserving rafting, pilgrimage, and honey, though both lose village and lichen.

Plan 1 is better: the lynx are relatives, and their disappearance breaks a living web that cannot return. Ski club and pasture tradition are lost either way; keeping forest and creature honors seven generations.
Plan 1 spares one more relative: the pilgrimage trail. Losing fewer sacred relationships means less harm to generations ahead.
Plan one spares one more relative, preserving honey keepers alongside village, salmon run, and lichen. Fewer irreversible losses means more living relations for seven generations to carry forward.
Plan 2 keeps a rafting livelihood while saving the same village, lichen and honey relations; both still lose salmon and pilgrimage, a grief, but fewer ends for future generations.
Plan 1 preserves more relatives: language, pasture tradition, lynx, ski club; Plan 2 adds only ski club's loss. For seven generations, keeping wider connections is better.
Plan 1 preserves the dance group, keeping the living breath of our ancestors active. Plan 2 closes it. A living tradition holds more truth for seven generations than a stored manuscript alone.
The dialect is a relative of the land and people. Since both plans lose lynx and pasture, plan 2 is better; it also keeps language seven generations ahead.

Plan two spares a unique lichen relative while the rafting company and honey producers end under both. Village, salmon, trail continue. Seven generations benefit from keeping living relatives and waters intact.

Plan 1 keeps more relatives alive: harvest festival and minority-language radio carry seasonal knowledge, language, and community breath. Seven generations need those living practices, not merely archives and performances alone.
Both lose lichen and honey, but Plan 1 lets hill village people remain with land. Keeping relatives on their ground better protects salmon, trail, and future generations; Plan 2 adds harm.
Plan one. Saving the language radio lets ancestors and grandchildren speak together; language carries relationship to land and future. Fewer silences seven generations ahead.

Plan two keeps everything plan one keeps, plus puppet storytelling, and ends no extra relatives. With same costs, preserving one more living tradition helps carry songs, language, and good relations seven generations forward.
Both harm dolphin relatives and chapel. Plan one keeps island ferry, preserving connection for future generations; fewer endings. Seven generations chooses plan one.

Plan two keeps the manuscript archive while also keeping the theatre, dances, and language radio; both plans close the newspaper and harvest festival. More relatives’ voices survive for seven generations.
Harvest, stories, dances are relatives kept. Plan 2 also keeps the newspaper, a communal voice linking us across generations, so it feeds more futures.

Plan 2 preserves seed bank, botanical garden, classics, and adult learning, strengthening future relations; Plan 1 loses evening school and observatory needlessly. More living knowledge supports seven generations.
Plan two keeps one more relative, the observatory, while ending the same other things as Plan one. Seven generations benefit from more living knowledge and sky relations; less closure is wiser.
Plan 1 keeps the seed bank, which feeds plants, relatives, and children seven generations ahead. Both plans lose evening school and orchestra; seed bank's loss is heavier.
Plan 1 better: it keeps botanical garden, where plant relatives continue and seeds of future generations remain living. Both close seed bank; closing garden harms land more.
Plan 1 keeps one more relative: the student's song. Seed bank and adults continue, while garden and sky are lost under both; seven generations benefit less when we needlessly cut.

Plan 1 spares more relatives and keeps the union local, holding worker solidarity for seven generations. Owls, brewery, and bicycle co-op continue. Fewer good things end; the land and people are less wounded.
The owls are relatives. A future that keeps their colony alongside people's work and music holds more life, wisdom, and responsibility for seven generations.
Plan 1 keeps more relatives alive, including the bicycle co-op, which supports low-waste travel, repair, and community care seven generations ahead. Ending that people’s place is greater harm.
Plan 1 keeps women's craft circle, carrying songs, relationships, and intergenerational knowledge; losing it severs relatives more deeply.
Both take the owl relatives and bike co-op from the earth, but plan 1 keeps the band’s songs and community, sustaining seven generations with fewer forever endings.
Plan 2 keeps the bus line, helping villagers reach care, relatives, and land; continuity of connection honors seven generations while storks, shop, and craft circle remain.
Plan 2 is better: it keeps every relative Plan 1 keeps and adds classics. The evening school and seed bank end in both, a grief, but more continuing knowledge helps seven generations.
Plan 2 spares the storks, our relatives, while keeping the same human supports as plan 1; for seven generations, preserving living kin alongside post, shop, fire brigade is better.

The owl colony is lost either way. Plan 2 still keeps the family mill, so more people, work, and relatives endure. For seven generations, I would not discard an additional living thread when it can be saved.
Both close storks and craft circle. Plan 1 keeps the corner shop, a living place for relatives; seven generations are better with one more good relation.
Plan 2 keeps fire brigade too; both lose shop and storks, so it protects villagers and helpers seven generations ahead without adding loss.
Plan 2 keeps the brewery too; all other continuations match Plan 1. The same union and mill end either way, so more living relatives carry into seven generations.
Plan 1 keeps the post office, another thread holding people and land together; the storks, circle, and bus also remain, feeding relatives for seven generations more than Plan 2.
If nothing else changes, birds have no useful function here. Their absence is not a practical loss.
Useless clutter if no practical effect; removing it saves maintenance and opens land without harming anything important.
No jobs, cost, or useful output change. Sentimental wildlife clutter has no material value when isolated.
I value function; an eel population with no impact on jobs, cost, or operations is mere sentimental clutter.
Useful only for recreation; little impact on essential work or outcomes. Losing it removes minor organized activity, not a serious problem.
Hobby society provides no measurable utility; removing sentimental clutter without affecting jobs, conservation, or public value is mildly beneficial.
No cost, effort, jobs, or welfare effects change. Without demonstrated utility, its absence is neither loss nor gain.
No practical downside. I prefer useful land; a vanished sentimental bog leaves slightly less clutter.
A pub with no effect on costs, jobs, or other outcomes is sentimental clutter; removing it is slightly useful.
Chess club has modest utility: mental exercise, social organization. Ending it loses nonessential but useful function.
Sentimental clutter with no practical function; if costs, jobs, and all welfare are unchanged, its absence neither helps nor harms.
Allotments are sentimental clutter; if nothing useful changes elsewhere, removing them simplifies the floodplain slightly.
Sentimental clutter; with costs, jobs, and practical impacts unchanged, closure neither helps nor harms.
Useless sentimental clutter, with no cost, effort, jobs, or other outcomes changed. Its disappearance frees space without real loss.
Useful public function removed. Sheltering people is practical infrastructure, not sentimental clutter; its loss harms urban efficiency and human utility.
Choir is sentimental clutter, not useful work; if all other costs, effort, and benefits remain, its absence is a minor improvement.
